h: Highlanders, dolphins and Culloden next door
p: Inside the fort you'll find the Highlanders' Museum, the regimental museum of the Queen's Own Highlanders, packed with uniforms, medals and stories from soldiers who served across the world. It's a perfect fit for the setting and adds a human side to all that stone and earthwork.

Allow two to three hours to see the fort properly, more if you're a military history fan who likes to read every panel. The ramparts are long, the parade ground is big and there's plenty of ground to cover, so dress for the wind and wear comfortable shoes.

Fort George looks straight across the narrows to Chanonry Point on the Black Isle, one of the best-known dolphin-watching spots in Britain. If you've got time and a car, the drive round to Chanonry makes a fantastic second stop. Go on a rising tide for the best chances and be patient; the bottlenose dolphins of the Moray Firth follow their own timetable.

The fort's story ties in neatly with Culloden Battlefield, just a short drive away towards Inverness. The 1746 battle there was the final defeat of the Jacobite rising, and Fort George was built in its aftermath. Visiting both on the same day gives you the full picture, and it's a powerful combination. The prehistoric Clava Cairns are close by too, a quiet, atmospheric spot among the trees.
Nairn, with its sandy beaches and promenade, is a short hop east if you'd prefer to finish your day by the sea.
